khanty_kul_otyr.name: takes the form of the diving bird that brings up the first silt
khanty_kul_otyr.notes: In the Ob-Ugric earth-diver cosmogony Kul-Otyr appears as the great diving bird (loon) that, at Num-Torum's command, fetches a lump of mud from beneath the primal water out of which the earth is spun.

sources.reference: K. F. Karjalainen, Die Religion der Jugra-Völker (FFC, 1921-1927)

khanty_kul_otyr.name: rules the disease-spirits (kulis) of the lower world
khanty_kul_otyr.notes: As lord of the underworld he commands the kuli/khul spirits of sickness, sending illness and death up to the human world through openings in the earth; black animals are sacrificed to avert him.

sources.reference: K. F. Karjalainen, Die Religion der Jugra-Völker (FFC, 1921-1927)

khanty_kaltes_ekwa.name: rocks the seven heavenly cradles to make each soul
khanty_kaltes_ekwa.notes: On the golden roof of her house she rocks seven cradles seven times, fashioning the soul that is born into a new child; an extension of her role as giver of children and fixer of each lifespan.

sources.reference: K. F. Karjalainen, Die Religion der Jugra-Völker (FFC, 1921-1927)

khanty_num_torum.name: sends the diving bird to raise the earth from the primal water
khanty_num_torum.notes: In the earth-diver cosmogony Num-Torum commands a diver (loon) to bring up silt from beneath the water; the silt spins and grows into the earth.

sources.reference: K. F. Karjalainen, Die Religion der Jugra-Völker (FFC, 1921-1927)

khasi_u_lei_shyllong.name: grants prosperity and a rich harvest when propitiated at Pomblang
khasi_u_lei_shyllong.notes: As the chief land-tutelary of the Khyrim (Nongkrem) state the god is propitiated by the Syiem and high priest for the prosperity, fertility and bumper harvest of the people at the annual Pomblang Nongkrem rite.

sources.reference: Government of Meghalaya, Nongkrem Dance (Ka Pomblang Nongkrem) cultural record

khasi_u_blei_nongthaw.name: governs the world through divine decree (Ka Hukum)
khasi_u_blei_nongthaw.notes: In Niam Khasi the formless creator orders the cosmos and the moral lives of people through Ka Hukum Blei, the divine decree, beneath which all the lesser gods and spirits exercise their power.

sources.reference: P. R. T. Gurdon, The Khasis (1907)

kiribati_na_kika.name: uses his eight octopus-arms to lift islands, beaches and rocks
kiribati_na_kika.notes: The octopus-god raises the new land from the sea-floor with his many arms during the ordering of the world, complementing Riiki the eel who lifts the sky.

sources.reference: Arthur Grimble, Tungaru Traditions (ed. H. E. Maude, 1989)

kiribati_naatibu.name: his eyes, brains and bones become sun, moon, stars and land
kiribati_naatibu.notes: When the primal being is slain the sun and moon are made from his eyes, the stars from his brains, and the islands from his bones and flesh - the Gilbertese world-from-body motif.

sources.reference: Arthur Grimble, Tungaru Traditions (ed. H. E. Maude, 1989)

kiribati_auriaria.name: is invoked as lord (uea) of the pandanus in fructification rites
kiribati_auriaria.notes: As the deity of the Karongoa clan and lord of the pandanus, Auriaria is the figure consulted in the rituals for the fruiting of the pandanus, his sacred tree.

sources.reference: Arthur Grimble, Tungaru Traditions (ed. H. E. Maude, 1989)
V. N. Chernetsov, in Studies in Siberian Shamanism (ed. Michael, 1963)

khoekhoe_heitsi_eibib.name: The cairn-graves of Heitsi-Eibib
khoekhoe_heitsi_eibib.notes: Travellers passing one of the many stone cairns reckoned the graves of the ever-dying, ever-reborn hero add a stone (or a twig or bit of food) and utter a prayer for rain, safe passage, health of cattle and protection against ||Gaunab; first-fruits were also deposited there before a journey or hunt.

sources.reference: Theophilus Hahn, Tsuni-||Goam: The Supreme Being of the Khoi-Khoi (1881)

khoekhoe_tsui_goab.name: Prayers for rain to Tsui-||Goab
khoekhoe_tsui_goab.notes: The Khoekhoe prayed to Tsui-||Goab for rain, thunder and the health of people and cattle, especially in drought; Hahn records the morning/rain prayers addressed to him as the dawn-god who dies and rises again.

sources.reference: Theophilus Hahn, Tsuni-||Goam: The Supreme Being of the Khoi-Khoi (1881)

khasi_u_lei_shyllong.name: Ka Pomblang Nongkrem (Nongkrem dance)
khasi_u_lei_shyllong.notes: The five-day Khyrim state festival at Smit: the Syiem of Khyrim and the high priest (Lyngdoh) offer oblation to U Lei Shyllong, sacrificing a cock and goats (pomblang), and maidens and warriors dance to secure a bumper harvest and the welfare of the state.

sources.reference: Government of Meghalaya, Nongkrem Dance (Ka Pomblang Nongkrem) cultural record

khasi_u_blei_nongthaw.name: Sacrifice and divination of the Niam Khasi
khasi_u_blei_nongthaw.notes: The indigenous Khasi religion offers animal sacrifice (cocks, goats) under the sovereignty of the creator U Blei Nongthaw to propitiate the spirits, with divination by cowries, breaking eggs and reading entrails to learn which spirit is offended.

sources.reference: P. R. T. Gurdon, The Khasis (1907)

khasi_ka_mei_ramew.name: Offerings to Mother Earth (Ka Mei Ramew)
khasi_ka_mei_ramew.notes: As the earth-mother whom the descended clans must steward, Ka Mei Ramew (Ka Mei Ram-ew) is honoured with propitiatory offerings before cultivation and at household rites of the Niam Khasi.

sources.reference: P. R. T. Gurdon, The Khasis (1907)

khmer_neak_ta.name: Loeung Neak Ta (raising/feeding the guardian)
khmer_neak_ta.cadence: annual, at the onset of the monsoon (rice-planting)
khmer_neak_ta.notes: Villagers gather at the spirit-hut shrine, set beneath a banyan or other sacred tree, with incense, fruit, cooked food and drink, praying for rain, good harvest, health and protection; a chosen medium may be possessed so the neak ta speaks and heals. The rite recurs yearly as farmers prepare to plant.

sources.reference: Ang Choulean, Les etres surnaturels dans la religion populaire khmere (1986)

kikuyu_ngai.name: Sacrifice at the mugumo (sacred fig)
kikuyu_ngai.notes: Elders sacrifice a lamb and a kid beneath a chosen mugumo (sacred fig) tree, pour the fat and blood on the trunk and offer the roasted meat to Ngai as a burnt offering, the people praying turned toward Kirinyaga (Mount Kenya); cutting a mugumo is taboo.

sources.reference: Jomo Kenyatta, Facing Mount Kenya (1938)

kirati_yuma_sammang.name: Chasok Tangnam (first-harvest festival)
kirati_yuma_sammang.notes: The Limbu first-harvest thanksgiving: the new crop is offered to Yuma Sammang and the other deities and ancestors before it may be eaten; the rites are conducted by the Phedangma priest reciting the Mundhum.

sources.reference: Chaitanya Subba, The Culture and Religion of Limbus (1995)

kirati_theba_sammang.name: Worship of Theba Sammang with Yuma
kirati_theba_sammang.cadence: in Limbu household and clan rites
kirati_theba_sammang.notes: As the paternal/ancestral war-deity Theba Sammang is honoured alongside Yuma Sammang in the rites recited by the Phedangma, the pair ranking second only to the high god Tagera Ningwaphuma.

sources.reference: Chaitanya Subba, The Culture and Religion of Limbus (1995)

kirati_paruhang.name: Sakela (Sakewa) offerings to the ancestral pair
kirati_paruhang.cadence: twice yearly (Ubhauli, Baisakh full moon; Udhauli, Mangsir full moon)
kirati_paruhang.notes: The Rai (Khambu) festival of Sakela/Sakewa honours nature and the ancestral creator-pair Paruhang and Sumnima with dance (Sakela sili) and offerings, praying for healthy crops and protection from calamity at the turn of the agricultural seasons.

sources.reference: Martin Gaenszle, Origins and Migrations: Kinship, Mythology and Ethnic Identity among the Mewahang Rai (2000)

kirati_sumnima.name: Sakela (Sakewa) offerings to the ancestral pair
kirati_sumnima.notes: The earth-mother Sumnima is honoured with her consort Paruhang at the Rai Sakela/Sakewa festival of seasonal renewal, the community dancing and offering for fertility of the soil and good harvest.

sources.reference: Martin Gaenszle, Origins and Migrations: Kinship, Mythology and Ethnic Identity among the Mewahang Rai (2000)

sacredAnimals.name: hare
sacredAnimals.notes: Her commonest theriomorphic form; she manifests as a hare, linking her to the moon and to renewal of life.

sources.reference: K. F. Karjalainen, Die Religion der Jugra-Völker (FFC, 1921-1927)

sacredAnimals.name: goose/bird-woman
sacredAnimals.notes: She also takes the shape of a bird (goose), the bird-woman form in which she descends and is invoked.

sources.reference: K. F. Karjalainen, Die Religion der Jugra-Völker (FFC, 1921-1927)

attributes.name: radiant horseman crossing the sky
attributes.notes: Depicted as a shining rider on his winged horse making a daily circuit of the heavens; his image is embroidered on the sacrificial horse-cloth.

sources.reference: K. F. Karjalainen, Die Religion der Jugra-Völker (FFC, 1921-1927)

sacredAnimals.name: goose/swan
sacredAnimals.notes: One of the shapes the World-Watching Man takes to move between the worlds; the goose is closely associated with his cult.

sources.reference: K. F. Karjalainen, Die Religion der Jugra-Völker (FFC, 1921-1927)

attributes.name: blackness
attributes.notes: The underworld lord is figured as black; the animals sacrificed to him are required to be black, in contrast with the bright upper-world gods.

sources.reference: K. F. Karjalainen, Die Religion der Jugra-Völker (FFC, 1921-1927)

attributes.name: the stone cairn-grave
attributes.notes: His defining marker: heaps of stones at mountain passes and roadsides across Namaland and the Northern Cape, each a place where he died and was reborn, to which passers add a stone.

sources.reference: Theophilus Hahn, Tsuni-||Goam: The Supreme Being of the Khoi-Khoi (1881)
Jomo Kenyatta, Facing Mount Kenya (1938)

sacredPlants.name: mugumo (sacred fig) of the first homestead
sacredPlants.notes: Gikuyu sacrifices under the mugumo fig at Mukurwe wa Nyagathanga to obtain husbands for his daughters; the fig grove is the founding shrine of the clans.

sources.reference: Jomo Kenyatta, Facing Mount Kenya (1938)

attributes.name: red-skinned giant
attributes.notes: Pre-eminent ancestor figured as a giant of red (sun-coloured) skin and red hair come from Samoa.

sources.reference: Arthur Grimble, Tungaru Traditions (ed. H. E. Maude, 1989)

sacredAnimals.name: rat (kimoa)
sacredAnimals.notes: His totem is the kimoa (rat), the dweller in the pandanus of which he is lord.

sources.reference: Arthur Grimble, Tungaru Traditions (ed. H. E. Maude, 1989)

sacredPlants.name: pandanus
sacredPlants.notes: Auriaria is the uea (lord) of the pandanus tree, the staple of the atolls.

sources.reference: Arthur Grimble, Tungaru Traditions (ed. H. E. Maude, 1989)

attributes.name: eyes that flash like lightning
attributes.notes: A red-haired woman whose eyes flash like lightning, the trait that links her to the storm.

sources.reference: Arthur Grimble, Tungaru Traditions (ed. H. E. Maude, 1989)

attributes.name: the Black Sky
attributes.notes: ||Gaunab dwells in and is identified with the dark/black sky from which he sends sickness and death, the cosmic opposite of the dawn-god's bright sky.

sources.reference: Theophilus Hahn, Tsuni-||Goam: The Supreme Being of the Khoi-Khoi (1881)
